title: Mira and the Loud Goose
markdown:
In a town of cobbles and hearth-bread, Mira the fox kept the museum as one keeps a sleeping relative: with beeswax, small brushes, and the dignity of not shouting. Her fur held the last of twilight. Her eyes, people said, had wells in them. At home Bea the goat filled the rooms with hoof-percussion and clover petals, an appetite that treated optimism as a food group.

This week the library—roof sagged like a tired beast, windows winking—prepared Literary Luminaries. Mira had offered, quietly, an exhibition of forgotten bookbinding. Somewhere under her ribs a small ambition sat like a warm coal: the Humble Artisan award, a prize so modest its trophy was often mistaken for a lustrous paperweight. She did not want a spotlight. She wanted a lamp left on.

The library, usually a hush of turning pages, now pulsed. Dust moted in the arches. Librarians, ordinarily as still as gargoyles, bustled. Lemon polish fought a floral arrangement that had tried too hard. Between the stacks Mira laid out her modest altar: needles, linen thread, a spine whose gold had gone the colour of weak tea. It was there she met Bartholomew, a goose of imposing plumage and the conviction that the universe ought to orbit his honk. He told anyone with ears that he was “optimising the flow of intellectual engagement,” which in practice meant rearranging furniture until it agreed with him.

Bea arrived smelling of lavender and dandelion salad. She nudged a stack of creamy programmes bound in sapphire ribbons that had ideas of their own. One pile tipped. Paper fled like startled pigeons.

“Fear not,” Bea said, with a glint that had never been accused of humility. “We are not yielding to disorder. We are expanding what a stack may mean.”

Bartholomew, meanwhile, orchestrated revelations. His honks filled the vaults. He insisted each award category be recited with interpretive wing-work that would have tired a tragedian. Mira tried to set a centuries-old binding—so fragile it seemed to flinch at air—and found herself perpetually outflanked. Bartholomew would decree that a display needed gravitas, then stand in front of it, chest out, a portrait of lunch well organised.

That was the first real hurdle. Mira’s exhibit had been made for looking. Bartholomew’s body was an eclipse.

“The Humble Artisan award,” he proclaimed, “shall be bestowed with a flourish befitting monarchs, and the sonorous fanfare of a precisely calibrated oboe!”

Mira’s quiet communion with old leather was being annexed by goose-led spectacle. She did not say so. She only shifted the binding an inch, as if an inch could survive a brass band.

Evening unfurled. Chandeliers made a kinder gold. Townsfolk arrived in a murmur like a hidden stream: bakers still dusted with flour, a schoolmistress with ink on her cuff, two visiting scholars who had come for the oboe and might yet remain for the leather. Ancient paper and beeswax did their old work. Bartholomew commandeered the microphone with the ease of a goose who had never doubted a lectern. He spoke of unseen currents of literary endeavour, cleared a throat surprisingly empty of bird, and rose to a thrilling crescendo.

“And now, the Humble Artisan! For those who toiled in quiet dedication, silent guardians of narratives!”

His magnificent wing swept toward Mira’s display as if it were a footnote to his own epic. Applause, thin and puzzled, followed the wing rather than the work. That was the second hurdle: not merely standing in front of the craft, but introducing it as scenery.

Mira had been poised to speak of stitches and tools. She stood instead in the lull his finale left, paws on a worn cover that still knew hands. She looked at the tooled leather, at the hours in it, at Bartholomew preening for a handful of bemused hats.

“Actually,” she said, and her voice carried without asking the rafters for help, “it is not so much about toiling, though there is that. It is the joy of making something beautiful that can endure. This binding—” she indicated the oldest, a silent monument—“was fashioned by a woman named Elara, nearly five centuries ago. She loved stories enough to want them held with reverence. That is all. Carefully wrought things keep their own power.”

A hush arrived that applause could not have bought. Bartholomew’s beak hung open, for once unemployed. There was no oboe. Only a fox telling the truth of a craft, and the room discovering it had wanted that more than fanfare.

The Humble Artisan medal, small and unpretentious, was given with a nod from the head librarian, whose eyes had understood all along. Mira felt its cool weight. Bea beamed from the edge, clover still in her coat. Bartholomew managed a stiff inclination of the head that was, against all odds, sincere.

Later the chandeliers dimmed. Mira set the medal beside Elara’s binding rather than in her pocket. The stitches, seen close, were still small acts of faith: a woman five centuries gone, keeping stories from falling apart in the hand. The paperweight-that-was-a-prize caught the last gold and did not need to be announced. Bartholomew, at a distance, practised a quieter honk, as if testing whether air could be used for listening. Bea ate a programme ribbon, considerately, and the library went back to being a place where pages might turn without accompaniment.
